Please write a three-sentence summary of this workplace story.

In the hospital records office, Aadhya's face never changed. When the auditor found an error, her expression stayed flat; when the team celebrated a clean audit, she nodded once. New colleague Ira read it as coldness and felt shut out. For weeks she guessed: was Aadhya bored, unimpressed or upset? Then Ira noticed patterns. Aadhya never missed a deadline, quietly fixed errors before anyone asked, and kept a list of everyone's birthdays. One Friday Ira said, "I can never tell what you're thinking. Are you okay with my work?" Aadhya paused and said, "Sorry. It's how I stay steady when things are busy. Your work is careful; I was going to tell you." Ira smiled, though she still couldn't read her face.

Ira thinks her colleague Aadhya is cold because her face never shows feeling. Then she notices how reliable and thoughtful Aadhya is, and asks her directly. Aadhya explains that staying calm helps her cope and says Ira's work is careful.

Briefly, how does Elizabeth now feel about Wickham?

Elizabeth was now to see Mr. Wickham for the last time. Having been frequently in company with him since her return, agitation was pretty well over; the agitations of former partiality entirely so. She had even learnt to detect, in the very gentleness which had first delighted her, an affectation and a sameness to disgust and weary. In his present behaviour to herself, moreover, she had a fresh source of displeasure; for the inclination he soon testified of renewing those attentions which had marked the early part of their acquaintance could only serve, after what had since passed, to provoke her. She lost all concern for him in finding herself thus selected as the object of such idle and frivolous gallantry; and while she steadily repressed it, could not but feel the reproof contained in his believing, that however long, and for whatever cause, his attentions had been withdrawn, her vanity would be gratified, and her preference secured, at any time, by their renewal.
Elizabeth no longer likes Wickham. His gentle charm now seems fake and dull to her, and she is annoyed that he tries to flirt with her again, as if she would be flattered.

How would you put this extract in one sentence?

I did not gain very much, however, by my inspection. Our visitor bore every mark of being an average commonplace British tradesman, obese, pompous, and slow. He wore rather baggy grey shepherd's check trousers, a not over-clean black frock-coat, unbuttoned in the front, and a drab waistcoat with a heavy brassy Albert chain, and a square pierced bit of metal dangling down as an ornament. A frayed top-hat and a faded brown overcoat with a wrinkled velvet collar lay upon a chair beside him. Altogether, look as I would, there was nothing remarkable about the man save his blazing red head, and the expression of extreme chagrin and discontent upon his features.
The visitor looks like a plain, heavy, pompous tradesman in rumpled clothes, with bright red hair and an annoyed look.

Summarize this text in three sentences.

So here's the funny part, looking back. In my first month at the firm, Pankaj sir barely said anything to me except things like "Fine" or "Send it by five." I decided he disliked me. Honestly, I was sure of it. So I, the only girl in that team, stopped talking in the huddles. I just nodded and took notes. Then at the end of the month he said to someone, not knowing I could hear, "Manjula doesn't seem very interested. Never asks anything." I was shocked. Not interested? I was terrified! And he wasn't disliking me, he was just like that with everyone, short and quick, because he had twelve projects. We'd each made up a story about the other. That's me, Manjula. Quiet does not mean bored, I learnt.

Manjula thought her new boss disliked her because he spoke so briefly, so she stopped speaking in team meetings. He, in turn, thought she was uninterested. In fact he was just busy with many projects, and she learned that being quiet does not mean being bored.

One-sentence summary of this, please.

"I wish I hadn't mentioned Dinah!" she said to herself in a melancholy tone. "Nobody seems to like her, down here, and I'm sure she's the best cat in the world! Oh, my dear Dinah! I wonder if I shall ever see you any more!" And here poor Alice began to cry again, for she felt very lonely and low-spirited. In a little while, however, she again heard a little pattering of footsteps in the distance, and she looked up eagerly, half hoping that the Mouse had changed his mind, and was coming back to finish his story.
Alice cries because nobody likes her cat Dinah, but she looks up hopefully when she hears footsteps, hoping the Mouse is back.

Tell this to a child in two sentences.

How our hydraulic engineer had been conveyed from the garden to the spot where he recovered his senses might have remained forever a mystery were it not for the soft mould, which told us a very plain tale. He had evidently been carried down by two persons, one of whom had remarkably small feet and the other unusually large ones. On the whole, it was most probable that the silent Englishman, being less bold or less murderous than his companion, had assisted the woman to bear the unconscious man out of the way of danger.

The footprints in the soft soil showed that two people carried the engineer from the garden, one with small feet and one with large. The Englishman probably helped the woman carry the unconscious man to safety, since he seemed less fierce than his partner.

What is Elizabeth saying? Just the main idea, in two sentences.

"And I certainly never shall give it. I am not to be intimidated into anything so wholly unreasonable. Your Ladyship wants Mr. Darcy to marry your daughter; but would my giving you the wished-for promise make their marriage at all more probable? Supposing him to be attached to me, would my refusing to accept his hand make him wish to bestow it on his cousin? Allow me to say, Lady Catherine, that the arguments with which you have supported this extraordinary application have been as frivolous as the application was ill-judged. You have widely mistaken my character, if you think I can be worked on by such persuasions as these. How far your nephew might approve of your interference in his affairs, I cannot tell; but you have certainly no right to concern yourself in mine. I must beg, therefore, to be importuned no further on the subject."

Elizabeth refuses to promise what Lady Catherine demands, saying that her promise would not make Darcy marry anyone else. She calls Lady Catherine's arguments foolish and her interference unfair, and asks not to be pressed any further.

Shrink this text to three sentences.

She perfectly remembered everything that had passed in conversation between Wickham and herself in their first evening at Mr. Philips's. Many of his expressions were still fresh in her memory. She was now struck with the impropriety of such communications to a stranger, and wondered it had escaped her before. She saw the indelicacy of putting himself forward as he had done, and the inconsistency of his professions with his conduct. She remembered that he had boasted of having no fear of seeing Mr. Darcy--that Mr. Darcy might leave the country, but that he should stand his ground; yet he had avoided the Netherfield ball the very next week. She remembered, also, that till the Netherfield family had quitted the country, he had told his story to no one but herself; but that after their removal, it had been everywhere discussed; that he had then no reserves, no scruples in sinking Mr. Darcy's character, though he had assured her that respect for the father would always prevent his exposing the son.

She recalls her first evening's talk with Wickham and now sees how improper it was for him to tell such things to a stranger. He had said he did not fear Mr. Darcy, yet he avoided the Netherfield ball. Once the Netherfield family left, he spoke openly against Mr. Darcy, though he had said respect for the father would stop him.

Summarize this text for a child in two sentences.

"Vaisampayana continued, 'Hearing these words, fraught with righteousness and merit, of that Brahmana and approving of them, every person in that assembly said, "Excellent, Excellent" and accepted them as his own. Dhritarashtra also, repeatedly applauding those words, slowly dismissed that assembly of his subjects. Thus honoured by them and looked upon with auspicious glances, the old king, O chief of Bharata's race, joined his hands and honoured them all in return. He then entered his own mansion with Gandhari. Listen now to what he did after that night had passed away.'"
Everyone in the meeting praises the Brahmana's good words, and the old king Dhritarashtra agrees. He thanks them with joined hands, sends them home, and goes into his house with Gandhari.

Fog had grounded every flight out of Lucknow, and Sonali's interview for the Bengaluru fellowship was at ten the next morning. Around her, people shouted at the airline desk. Her friend Nandini called. "What are you going to do?" Sonali took out a notebook and drew a line down the middle. On one side: the fog, the airline, the panel's decision. On the other: emailing the panel, checking the overnight train, preparing her answers. She emailed first, briefly and politely, asking about an online interview. She booked a train seat as a backup. Then she sat on her suitcase and practised her answers aloud. "And if they say no?" Nandini asked. "Then I'll have done what I could." Her stomach still fluttered, but her voice was calm. At midnight, the reply came: online would be fine.

Three-sentence summary of this passage, please.

Fog cancels every flight out of Lucknow the night before Sonali's fellowship interview in Bengaluru, so she lists what she can and cannot control. She emails the panel politely about an online interview, books a backup train seat, and practises her answers aloud. At midnight the panel replies that an online interview is fine.

One-line summary of this extract, please.

"I will not be interrupted! Hear me in silence. My daughter and my nephew are formed for each other. They are descended, on the maternal side, from the same noble line; and, on the father's, from respectable, honourable, and ancient, though untitled, families. Their fortune on both sides is splendid. They are destined for each other by the voice of every member of their respective houses; and what is to divide them?--the upstart pretensions of a young woman without family, connections, or fortune! Is this to be endured? But it must not, shall not be! If you were sensible of your own good, you would not wish to quit the sphere in which you have been brought up."
The speaker declares that the speaker's daughter and nephew are meant for each other, and no young woman without family or fortune may divide them.

I'm Disha, Sudha's classmate, and I watched her do something I wouldn't have thought of. We both went to a one-day energy conference in Chennai. At lunch she pointed at a speaker, Dr Iyer, and said, 'Everyone will send him a thank-you. What would actually help him?' She had heard him say he'd miss the afternoon panel because of a flight. So during that panel she took careful notes, and that night she wrote a one-page summary of the three main arguments and the audience questions. I saw her cut it twice to keep it short. She emailed it to him the next morning, with one line: 'You mentioned missing this panel, so I thought this might be useful.' He wrote back the same day, thanked her, and asked about her own project. They've exchanged messages every few weeks since. I can't know what she felt, but she read his first reply aloud to me twice.

Write a two-sentence summary of this section.

Disha describes how classmate Sudha helped Dr Iyer, who missed a panel, by writing and emailing him a short summary. He replied that day, thanked her and asked about her project, and they still write every few weeks.

I hoped heartily we should have peace now. It hurt me to think the master should be made uncomfortable by his own good deed. I fancied the discontent of age and disease arose from his family disagreements; as he would have it that it did: really, you know, sir, it was in his sinking frame. We might have got on tolerably, notwithstanding, but for two people—Miss Cathy, and Joseph, the servant: you saw him, I daresay, up yonder. He was, and is yet most likely, the wearisomest self-righteous Pharisee that ever ransacked a Bible to rake the promises to himself and fling the curses to his neighbours. By his knack of sermonising and pious discoursing, he contrived to make a great impression on Mr. Earnshaw; and the more feeble the master became, the more influence he gained. He was relentless in worrying him about his soul's concerns, and about ruling his children rigidly. He encouraged him to regard Hindley as a reprobate; and, night after night, he regularly grumbled out a long string of tales against Heathcliff and Catherine: always minding to flatter Earnshaw's weakness by heaping the heaviest blame on the latter.

Could you recap this section for me? Three sentences is enough.

The narrator hoped for peace and believes the master's unhappiness came from his failing health, not family quarrels. The real trouble came from Miss Cathy and Joseph, a self-righteous servant who gained influence over the weakening Mr. Earnshaw. Joseph nagged him about his soul, urged harsh rule of his children, and nightly blamed Heathcliff and Catherine.

In under 70 words, what happens in this excerpt?

The Dasara dolls were already arranged on the wooden steps in the front room when Vidya's interview letter came from the government school in Hassan. 'They'll take someone from the city,' she told her brother Darshan, and slid the letter under the calendar. For the nine days of the festival she strung marigolds, handed out sundal to the neighbours' children, and opened her teaching notes only once, on the last night, turning pages without reading them. On the early bus to Hassan her hands were cold. When the panel asked how she would teach fractions to a class that was struggling, something she had done for the neighbours' children all summer, her mind went blank. She mumbled, apologised twice, and left before they finished. At home she dropped onto the mat and told Darshan, 'See? I knew it.' Darshan picked up the notes, still crisp and unmarked, and said nothing for a long moment.
Vidya hides her interview letter, then blanks on a fractions question at the Hassan interview, leaves early and tells her brother she knew it.

Suta continued, "I have now told you all that Vaisampayana recited to Janamejaya. Having listened to Vaisampayana's narration, king Janamejaya properly discharged all his duties according to the ordinances laid down in the scriptures. Ye have all undergo very severe penances and observed many high and excellent vows. Residing in this sacred forest that is known by the name of Naimisha, ye are foremost of all persons conversant with the Vedas. Ye foremost of regenerate ones, ye all have come to this great sacrifice of Saunaka. Do ye all adore and worship that Eternal and Supreme Lord of the universe in excellent sacrifices, properly pouring libations of clarified butter into the fire with the aid of mantras and dedicating the same unto Narayana. As regards myself, I heard this excellent narrative that has descended from generation to generation, from my sire who recited it to me in former times."

Say in three sentences what this short passage is saying.

Suta has now told all that Vaisampayana told King Janamejaya, who then carried out his duties as the scriptures direct. Suta tells the sages gathered at Saunaka's great sacrifice in Naimisha forest to worship the Supreme Lord with offerings and mantras. Suta's own father recited the story long ago, and it has passed down through the generations.

"'"Brahman said, 'Excellent is this question, ye highly blessed ones! It is at once auspicious and high and fraught with a mystery. This question that ye have put is subtil and is fraught with high benefit to mankind. Ye Rishis possessed of wealth of penances, I shall recite everything to you in detail. Do ye listen with attention to what I say as to how men acquire the merits attaching to sacrifices (even when they are unable to perform them through poverty.) In the lighted fortnight of the month of Pausha, when the constellation Rohini is in conjunction, if one, purifying oneself by a bath, lies under the cope of heaven, clad in a single piece of raiment, with faith and concentrated attention, and drinks the rays of the moon, one acquires the merits that attach to the performance of great sacrifices. Ye foremost of regenerate persons, this is a high mystery that I declare unto you in reply to your questions, ye that are possessed of insight into the subtil truths of all topics of enquiry.'"'"

Two sentences, please: what is this section about?

Brahman praises the question and says Brahman will explain how poor people can gain the merit of sacrifices without performing them. In Pausha, bathing, lying under the open sky and drinking the moon's rays with faith earns the merit of great sacrifices.

Shrink this piece to three sentences.

When my father returned from Milan, he found playing with me in the hall of our villa a child fairer than pictured cherub—a creature who seemed to shed radiance from her looks and whose form and motions were lighter than the chamois of the hills. The apparition was soon explained. With his permission my mother prevailed on her rustic guardians to yield their charge to her. They were fond of the sweet orphan. Her presence had seemed a blessing to them, but it would be unfair to her to keep her in poverty and want when Providence afforded her such powerful protection. They consulted their village priest, and the result was that Elizabeth Lavenza became the inmate of my parents' house—my more than sister—the beautiful and adored companion of all my occupations and my pleasures.

When the narrator's father returns from Milan, he finds a lovely child playing with the narrator in the hall of the villa. The narrator's mother persuades the child's village guardians to let her go, so she need not live in poverty. Elizabeth Lavenza then joins the family as the narrator's more than sister and dear companion.

Can you explain this reading for a child? Two sentences, please.

The month of May had already commenced, and I expected the letter daily which was to fix the date of my departure, when Henry proposed a pedestrian tour in the environs of Ingolstadt, that I might bid a personal farewell to the country I had so long inhabited. I acceded with pleasure to this proposition: I was fond of exercise, and Clerval had always been my favourite companion in the ramble of this nature that I had taken among the scenes of my native country.
It is May, and the narrator expects a letter about the departure date. Henry suggests a walking tour, and the narrator happily agrees.

As soon as she had made out the proper way of nursing it, (which was to twist it up into a sort of knot, and then keep tight hold of its right ear and left foot, so as to prevent its undoing itself,) she carried it out into the open air. "If I don't take this child away with me," thought Alice, "they're sure to kill it in a day or two: wouldn't it be murder to leave it behind?" She said the last words out loud, and the little thing grunted in reply (it had left off sneezing by this time). "Don't grunt," said Alice; "that's not at all a proper way of expressing yourself."

I'd like this reading in three sentences.

Alice works out how to nurse the baby by twisting it into a knot, and carries it into the open air. She thinks leaving it would be murder, since they would surely kill it within a day or two. The baby grunts, and Alice tells it that is no proper way to speak.

Capture this short passage in three sentences.

Forty minutes before the chief guest arrived, Nikita, the fest's stage coordinator, stood under the lighting frame with her torch and didn't like what she saw. On the left, two metal clamps were missing, and a length of rope had been tied in their place. The frame dipped slightly towards the crowd barrier, where students were already packing in. Arnab, the lighting vendor, waved from the console. "It's held for three shows this month, madam. Don't worry." Nikita didn't raise her voice. "Arnab, two clamps are missing on the left, it's tied with rope, and it leans over the front row. I can't open the gates like this. Switch off the left bank, we move the barrier back three metres, and your crew fits clamps before the band." He sighed. "The chief guest is coming." "Then let's start now," she said. His crew found the clamps in the van. By the time the band came on, the frame stood straight.

Forty minutes before the chief guest arrives, Nikita finds clamps missing from the lighting frame, replaced with rope, with the frame leaning over the front row. She calmly asks vendor Arnab to switch off the left lights, move the barrier back and fit clamps before the band. His crew finds clamps in the van, and the frame stands straight when the band comes on.
